read: partial: main text pp. 1-9 in full (abstract, introduction, LSR-Transform and LSR-Synth construction, evaluation, experiments, analysis, related work, conclusion); appendix A.1-A.2 openings (pp. 11-13), B (pp. 14-16) and D (pp. 20-21) read; appendix C (implementation and prompts) not read
venue_now: ICML 2025, PMLR 267 (p. 1 footer); the file is arXiv 2504.10415v2, 7 Jun 2025
what_it_is: A benchmark for LLM-based scientific equation discovery (symbolic regression): given a dataset and a scientific description, a method must find the governing equation (p. 1-3). Its 239 problems are built so the target law cannot simply be recalled: 111 LSR-Transform problems rewrite 100 Feynman physics equations into less common forms by solving for a different variable with SymPy, and 128 LSR-Synth problems combine known terms with LLM-proposed synthetic terms in chemistry, biology, physics and materials science, checked by numerical solvers, a GPT-4o novelty check and two subject-matter experts (p. 3-5). Discovered equations are scored for symbolic accuracy by a GPT-4o judge (94.6% agreement with two authors on 130 problems) and for numeric fit on in-domain and out-of-domain data (p. 5, p. 15). Four discovery methods on three LLM backbones are compared; the best reaches 31.5% symbolic accuracy (p. 1, p. 3, p. 5-6).
domain: scientific equation discovery across chemistry (reaction kinetics), biology (population growth), physics (Feynman equations, damped harmonic oscillators) and materials science (stress-strain) (p. 3-5)
size: 239 problems: 111 LSR-Transform (all physics, from 100 Feynman equations) and 128 LSR-Synth (chemistry 36, biology 24, physics 43, materials science 25) (p. 3-5); four methods (LLM-SR, LaSR, SGA, data-blind prompting) x three backbones (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o-mini), 1,000 LLM calls per problem (p. 5-6)
source_of_items: perturbed from an existing set (Feynman benchmark equations transformed with SymPy, descriptions rewritten by GPT-4o, p. 3-4) and generated (GPT-4o-proposed known and synthetic terms, solver-checked, novelty-checked by GPT-4o, validated by two subject-matter experts, data from numerical solvers, p. 4-5)
instances: static set built by perturbation (LSR-Transform) and LLM-assisted synthesis (LSR-Synth); not regenerated per evaluation
has_gold_traces: no: the gold object is the ground-truth equation with its data; there are no intermediate solution steps, and the methods' search trajectories are not scored
evaluation: expression-level: symbolic accuracy, GPT-4o judging equivalence of the discovered and ground-truth equations after constants are replaced by placeholders; data fidelity by accuracy to tolerance (Acc_0.1) and NMSE on in-domain and, for LSR-Synth, out-of-domain test data (p. 5, p. 7, p. 14-15)
human_validation: LSR-Synth equations and plots of their data were cross-checked by two subject-matter experts for plausibility (p. 5). The GPT-4o symbolic-accuracy judge was checked against two authors on 130 randomly sampled problems: 94.6% agreement, 123 of 130 (p. 5, p. 15).
contamination_measures: perturbations: LSR-Transform rewrites well-known equations into less common forms and drops problems an LLM solves without the data (p. 3-4); LSR-Synth adds synthetic terms checked for novelty (p. 5); a data-blind prompting baseline gauges memorisation (p. 6); Figure 1 contrasts memorisation-like error curves on Feynman problems with the new sets (p. 1)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: 'Qualitative' contradicts the paper. LLM-SRBench is a symbolic-regression benchmark: a method must output a mathematical equation that fits the data (p. 1-3), scored by symbolic accuracy (equivalence judged by GPT-4o) and by numeric fidelity, Acc_0.1 and NMSE on in-domain and out-of-domain data (p. 5). By task it is the most symbolic of the six papers in the paragraph. S-P2 is also wrong for it: LSR-Synth spans chemistry, biology, physics and materials science (p. 4-5), and the task is data-driven discovery, not theoretical physics. The citation points at the right paper; the characterisation is wrong.

suggested_wording: LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025) targets scientific equation discovery, rewriting Feynman physics equations into less familiar forms and adding synthetic terms to known chemistry, biology, physics and materials models so that the target law cannot simply be recalled.
facts_to_cite: 239 equation-discovery problems: 111 LSR-Transform problems derived from 100 Feynman physics equations and 128 LSR-Synth problems in chemistry (36), biology (24), physics (43) and materials science (25) (p. 3-5).
LSR-Transform solves each Feynman equation for a different variable with SymPy and excludes problems an LLM can solve without the data, to test reasoning beyond memorised forms (p. 3-4).
LSR-Synth combines known terms with LLM-generated synthetic terms, checked for solvability with numerical solvers, for novelty by GPT-4o and for plausibility by two subject-matter experts (p. 4-5).

Symbolic accuracy is judged by GPT-4o, which agreed with two authors on 94.6% of 130 sampled problems (123 of 130) (p. 5, p. 15); numeric fit is measured by Acc_0.1 and NMSE on in-domain and out-of-domain data (p. 5, p. 7).
The best method reaches 31.5% symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform and 28.1% on LSR-Synth (p. 1, p. 3).
It benchmarks LLM-based discovery methods (LLM-SR, LaSR, SGA and data-blind prompting) on three backbones, each allowed 1,000 LLM calls per problem (p. 5-6).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: construction designed to defeat memorisation by transforming known problems and synthesising new terms (p. 3-5), the same concern behind EngTrace's generated instances; an LLM judge (GPT-4o) whose verdicts were checked against two authors on 130 problems (94.6%, p. 5, p. 15), a small precedent for EngTrace's expert validation of its residual judge; expert plausibility checks (p. 5); domains that touch EngTrace's chemical (reaction kinetics) and mechanical (stress-strain) branches (p. 4). Lacks: a problem-solving format (the task is fitting an equation to data with search methods, p. 2-5); instances generated at evaluation time (a fixed set of 239); gold traces; step-level evaluation (it scores the final equation's symbolic equivalence and data fit, p. 5); an engineering framing.
notes: The 'qualitative' label may be a swap within S-P1: by task LLM-SRBench is the most symbolic of the four 'symbolic or qualitative' citations, and ABench-Physics, labelled symbolic, is numeric-only. The domain counts on p. 3 (36/24/43/25) are LSR-Synth's 128 only; LSR-Transform's 111 are all physics, so 154 of 239 problems are physics (my arithmetic). The May reference list misprints four of six given names (citation_context_map.md). Scores come from discovery pipelines with 1,000 LLM calls per problem, so they are not comparable with single-pass benchmark accuracies. Besides the physical-sciences paragraph, it could serve the planned judge-validity paragraph as an example of an LLM judge validated on a small author-labelled sample. Confidence is high on the verdict and medium on keeping it rather than dropping it: its task is far from EngTrace's.
